title: Breakdown of Local Denoising as Semantic Speciation
authors: Guangkuo Liu, Mert Okyay, Yifan F. Zhang, Fangjun Hu, Rahul Nandkishore, Xun Gao
abstract: The dynamics of generative models exhibit two apparently distinct temporal windows: a speciation window, in which a sample commits to a semantic class, and a nonlocality window, in which local context windows become insufficient for generation. Motivated by evidence of their near-concurrence in a variety of frontier models, we investigate their relationship through the spatial distribution of semantic information. Under a "common cause" hypothesis, we prove that the nonlocality window must lie in the speciation window. This hypothesis postulates that semantic labels explain a fraction of the correlations between distant tokens, a condition that is natural for many real datasets. We further give conditions under which both windows shrink to a single limiting time as system size grows, defining a "phase transition", and verify this behavior analytically in Gaussian mixtures. Together, these results identify conditions under which semantic information explains the concurrence of speciation and nonlocality, connecting two complementary perspectives on the emergence of semantic structure in generative modeling.
summary: This theoretical paper connects the concepts of semantic structure emergence and the breakdown of local information processing in generative models. It proves that when semantic labels are the common cause of correlations, the failure of local denoising must occur within the period where the model commits to a semantic class. The work provides analytical conditions for these two distinct temporal windows to merge into a single phase transition.
main_problem: The paper investigates the relationship between two temporal dynamics in generative models: the 'speciation window' (semantic commitment) and the 'nonlocality window' (failure of local context).
main_result: Under a 'common cause' hypothesis, the nonlocality window must be contained within the speciation window, and conditions are derived for both windows to merge into a single 'phase transition'.
method: The analysis uses information-theoretic tools, specifically Mutual Information (MI) and Conditional Mutual Information (CMI), applied to theoretical models and analytically verified in Gaussian mixtures.
model_or_system: The study focuses on generative models, including diffusion and autoregressive models, analyzing their dynamics through the lens of semantic information structure.
key_observables: Speciation Window, Nonlocality Window, Mutual Information (MI), Conditional Mutual Information (CMI), and the breakdown of local denoising quantified by I(A; C | B).
important_parameters: Diffusion time $t$ (ranging from 0 to 1), system size $N$, and the signal-to-noise ratio $K_R$.
main_assumptions: The central assumption is the 'common cause' hypothesis, which posits that semantic labels explain a fraction of the correlations between distant tokens.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates that semantic speciation locates the window where local denoising breaks down, showing the denoising trajectory. Figure 2 shows that semantic conditioning reduces the average local–global prediction gap.
paper_structure: The paper first formally defines the two windows using information theory, then develops the common-cause hypothesis, and finally proves the containment relationship and the conditions for the phase transition using analytical calculations in Gaussian mixtures.
why_interesting: While the core subject is ML, the rigorous mathematical framework involving phase transitions, information bounds, and the analysis of local vs. global correlations mirrors concepts used in critical phenomena and disordered systems.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

The upper panel depicts a semantic speciation from white noise to cat or dog for local region (blue) and global region (magenta); the corresponding thresholds define a speciation window (black vertical lines). The noisy images in the window depict generation times in which the semantic identity is visible in the whole image, but invisible in a local patch (blue box). Figure 2: Semantic conditioning reduces the average local–global prediction gap in SD3. A smaller conditional gap means that restricting distant image-token interactions changes the model prediction less when semantic information is supplied. This is consistent with the common-cause interpretation: the description explains part of the shared image structure that would otherwise require distant context.

Figure 3: Label–reconstruction similarity remains high at early diffusion times and then falls toward zero. The sharp drop occurs first for the 64 × 64 crop, then for the 128 × 128 crop, and last for the full image.

Fig. 4(a) tracks the four mutual informations It(S; B), It(S; AB), It(S; BC), It(S; ABC). These curves are monotone decreasing under the forward diffusion dynamics and develop sharp late- time cliffs. The smaller regions lose semantic information earlier, while the global regions remain informative until later times. This is the finite-size numerical signature of the forward-backward semantic transition.

Fig. 4(b) plots the two conditional gaps It(S; A|B) = It(S; AB) −It(S; B), and It(S; A|BC) = It(S; ABC)−It(S; BC). These gaps peak near the steepest parts of the corresponding MI cliffs. For the parameters used here, Gloc peaks near t ≃0.88, whereas Gglob is smaller and delayed, peaking near t ≃0.94. This delay reflects the greater robustness of the global context ABC to the forward noise.
